text: Daoism began in China more than 2,000 years ago, with a book called the Daodejing.
According to tradition, it was written by Laozi, the Old Master, who wrote down his teaching as he rode west.
src: Daoism grew from the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi, works of the Warring States period / as a philosophy in the Warring States period (4th–3rd centuries BCE)
Tradition names Laozi, “the Old Master”, as its founder / rode west through the Hangu Pass and, at the request of its guardian, wrote down his teaching

text: A second book, the Zhuangzi, is full of witty stories.
In one, the thinker Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly, and then cannot tell which he really is.
src: whose witty and paradoxical stories mock conventional values and celebrate freedom
the famous dream in which Zhuangzi cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamt he was a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he is a man

text: Daoists follow the Dao, the Way, and try to act gently, like water, which gives way yet wears away stone.
Some tried to live very long lives through breathing exercises, meditation and making special mixtures called elixirs.
src: the Dao, the Way: the nameless source of the universe / like water, which yields to everything yet wears away the hardest stone

Its practitioners aimed to prolong life and to become xian, “immortals” or transcendents, through diet, breathing exercises, gymnastics, meditation and alchemy / the preparation of elixirs from minerals

text: More than 1,800 years ago, Daoists say, Zhang Daoling received a message from the god Laozi on a mountain in Sichuan.
He founded a religion with priests, rituals and gods, called the Way of the Celestial Masters.
src: Zhang Daoling, who in 142, according to its tradition, received a revelation on a mountain in Sichuan from Lord Lao, the deified Laozi
founded the Way of the Celestial Masters / it became an organised religion of priests, rituals, scriptures and gods

text: Many emperors supported Daoism, and later Wang Chongyang started an order of monks and nuns called Complete Perfection.
In the last century Chinese governments closed or destroyed many temples, but since the 1980s Daoism has come back.
src: emperors, above all the Tang, who claimed Laozi as their ancestor, patronised it / Wang Chongyang founded in 1167 the school of Complete Perfection, Quanzhen / The monks and nuns of Complete Perfection

Daoism suffered from campaigns against “superstition” in the Republic and in the People’s Republic of China / when temples were closed or destroyed / Since the 1980s Daoism, one of the five religions officially recognised in China, has revived

text: Daoism shaped Chinese poetry, painting and medicine.
Today millions of people practise taijiquan, a martial art of gentle movement, every morning in parks.
src: It shaped Chinese medicine, painting, poetry, alchemy and the martial arts
The martial art of taijiquan / is practised by millions of people every morning in the parks of China and across the world / gentle movement
